A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same multilingual prompting framework, renamed from EMCEI to EMCEE. All 18 pages of v1 and 21 pages of v2, including appendices, are readable and support reliable matching of methods, results and displays.

before.justification: v1 reports original LLM evaluations on four multilingual benchmarks and GlobalOpinionQA, along with component ablations and qualitative results.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical evaluations and adds retrieval comparisons, cost measurements, model evaluations and further ablations.

M1.justification: The main extraction, English-CoT and culturally conditioned judge pipeline remains unchanged despite renaming. v2 additionally introduces EMCEE(Route), a limited inference variant that selects the extraction or reasoning pathway from the query instead of comparing both generated responses (Table 1, Section 3.2).

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate M3-Exam, MKQA, XNLI, XCOPA and GlobalOpinionQA with the same represented languages and countries. The corrections from eight to nine MKQA languages and 36 to 34 countries reconcile counts with existing lists; they do not establish changed coverage. New model and ablation experiments reuse these tasks.

E2.justification: v2 adds evaluated RAG(NATIVE), RAG(ENG) and EMCEE(Route) comparators across the four main benchmarks (Table 1), plus ADAPTIVE contextual reasoning in Appendix B.5. These substantially expand comparison beyond the retained translation, instruction-language and CoT baselines.

E3.justification: New protocols include Qwen3-8B think-mode controls, Aya-8B evaluation on 400 examples, and adaptive/extraction-language comparisons on 800 examples each. v2 also introduces top-1 retrieval truncated to 100 words and a three-CoT cost control. Table 1 specifies top/bottom-half resource groups, including 7/7 for XNLI, whereas v1 describes a mean threshold; v2 Section 3.1 still retains that conflicting description. Baseline prompt templates also change, without establishing that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds analyses of routing versus merging, adaptive versus unconditional extraction, extraction instruction language, computational cost and think-mode, plus misleading or unnecessary extracted-context cases (Appendix C.1). Conversely, v1 Table 4's numerical language-cue ablation is removed, although its discussion survives in Appendix B.2. GlobalOpinionQA and the original success examples are retained through relocation.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated evaluation runs, seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests or uncertainty estimates. The additional sampled CoT paths are inference controls, not repeated-run uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial retrieval, routing, cost, model and ablation results while retaining the four main EMCEE All scores: 77.4, 52.3, 74.3 and 92.0. XNLI High/Low scores change from 75.4/72.8 to 74.7/73.9 alongside revised grouping; several component-ablation values also change. Language-cue result rows disappear. New Table 19 reports GPT-4o ENG-CoT at 82.9 and Llama EMCEE at 56.9, conflicting with 82.4 and 57.6 retained in Table 3; these are not established same-setting performance changes.

T1.justification: Neither version develops formal assumptions, propositions, proofs or mathematical derivations for the proposed framework. The revision remains empirical and conceptual.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion broaden the contribution framing from cultural explanations to synthetic query-relevant knowledge, including linguistic and domain context, combined with reasoning. The central two-stage contribution and multilingual improvement claims remain. The introductory low-resource improvement figure changes from 32.0% to 31.7%.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations favoring response-based merging over routing, internal context over retrieval, and extraction over think-mode, plus concrete misleading-context failure conditions. It removes v1's explicit limitation concerning severely underrepresented cultures. Some new interpretations exceed their evidence: Appendix B.4 claims Aya improvement across all four languages, although Table 16 shows Italian accuracy of 40 versus baseline scores of 45 and 46.

D1.justification: v2 supplies explicit resource-group memberships, retrieval settings, an adaptive system prompt, and token/cost measurements. It clarifies GPT-4o's role in generating exemplar answers and corrects dataset counts. However, v1's project-code availability statement and link disappear; the PDFs do not establish whether the repository itself became unavailable.

R1.justification: v2 more explicitly positions the framework as self-contained synthetic context extraction relative to retrieval augmentation, while retaining most prior-work connections. It adds Aya, Qwen documentation and Meta's Llama documentation references, and removes references including Wang et al.'s cultural-dominance study and Wei et al.'s CoT paper.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, method explanation, related work and conclusion undergo extensive rewriting around synthetic context and knowledge–reasoning integration. Compatibility results move into the analyses section; language-cue and steerability discussions move to Appendix B. Appendices gain a substantially reorganized analysis structure, failure-case discussion and AI-writing disclosure.

P2.justification: Figure 1 replaces the XLT illustration with retrieval augmentation, and Table 1 expands with comparator rows and subgroup counts. v2 adds cost, model, protocol and full-result tables and two failure-case figures, removes the numerical language-cue table, and extensively relocates appendix displays. Retained benchmark plots preserve their results after matching the reordered Arabic/Vietnamese groups.

improvement.justification: The added routing, adaptive-extraction and instruction-language controls strengthen evidence for the two-stage design beyond v1's component ablation. Retrieval/cost comparisons and failure cases also improve assessment of its scope. The net gain is limited by removal of numerical language-cue evidence and code-access information, conflicting resource-group definitions and Tables 3/19 scores, and the unsupported claim of improvement across all Aya languages. These reporting problems weaken otherwise useful additions.
